[THOUGHT] 
This 31‑year‑old woman has 5 months of intermittent flank pain without urinary symptoms, systemic signs, or objective urinary abnormalities: normal urinalysis with microscopy and a normal urine pregnancy test. She has a history of recurrent UTIs but no current dysuria, frequency, hematuria, or fever to suggest active infection or pyelonephritis. Nephrolithiasis (acute ureteral colic) would usually produce severe, colicky pain often radiating to groin and commonly associated with microscopic or gross hematuria; that is not described and the UA is normal. Chronic renal causes (e.g., chronic pyelonephritis, renal mass) would more likely show reproducible abnormal urinalysis or other systemic findings and often progressive course. Gynecologic causes (e.g., ovarian pathology, endometriosis) are possible but the patient does not report a cyclical pattern and no pelvic findings are documented.

The pain is intermittent over months, nonfocal on exam (no reproducible CVA tenderness on percussion), and lacks red flags. This pattern is most consistent with a musculoskeletal source — e.g., paraspinal/costovertebral myofascial pain or somatic pain from the posterior thoracolumbar structures (including costovertebral joint dysfunction). Musculoskeletal flank pain commonly causes intermittent, nonvisceral pain that is not accompanied by urinary abnormalities.

Therefore the single most likely diagnosis is musculoskeletal (costovertebral/paraspinal) flank pain — myofascial or joint dysfunction.

[DIAGNOSIS]
Musculoskeletal flank pain (costovertebral/paraspinal myofascial or joint dysfunction)
